opportunities.gap: The MDX body and the misconceptions file contradict each other on the most load-bearing point of the section. The MDX consistently frames printed text as loading the VISUAL channel because it 'enters through the eyes' (lines 26, 62, 78, 88, and the step-reveal answerIndex). But the misconceptions file (cma_channels_are_modalities, feedback field) says printed text 'is processed in the VERBAL channel, the same route used for narration.' These are two different and mutually exclusive readings of Mayer's dual-channel model (the sensory-modality interpretation vs the presentation-mode interpretation). A learner who reads both will be confused about which channel printed text loads. Mayer's canonical treatment uses the sensory-modality interpretation for channel definition (eyes->visual/pictorial channel, ears->auditory/verbal channel), which is what the MDX uses; the misconception feedback as written is wrong and undercuts the entire section.

Also rename/rewrite the description, which currently says channels are NOT defined by sense organ, the opposite of what the MDX teaches. Reconcile the 'pattern' label too.

opportunities.gap: In 'Core Concept' the text describes backward fading as removing 'the last step first (the step closest to the goal, often the easiest to attempt)'. In the worked-examples literature, backward fading removes the LAST solution step first precisely because, in the canonical chain, the final step is typically the one whose schema is most established / can be attempted with most support remaining; the parenthetical 'often the easiest to attempt' is a loose justification that can mislead (the last step is not generically the easiest). The rationale stated could be sharpened to match the literature's actual reasoning (the learner works forward through given steps and only attempts the final, most-supported step).
opportunities.proposed_change: Tighten the parenthetical to the literature's rationale: backward fading withdraws the final step first so the learner studies all earlier steps as a worked model and only generates the last step from a fully supported position; as expertise grows, fading proceeds backward toward the first step. Avoid the unqualified claim that the last step is 'often the easiest to attempt.'

sources.cite: Cleveland, W. S., & McGill, R. (1984). Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(387), 531-554.

final_opportunities.gap: The worked-example markup (two adjacent tags: AboutProjects) is used throughout to justify the symptom that runaway blue 'swallows everything below' the nav. Under the HTML5 parsing spec, when the parser meets the SECOND start tag while the first is still open, it acts as if a end tag had been seen (invoking the adoption agency algorithm), implicitly closing the first anchor. So in THIS exact two-anchor block 'About' renders as its own closed link and the styling does NOT propagate to paragraphs below the nav. The strong 'swallows every paragraph below' effect specifically requires a single unclosed followed by NON-anchor content. A browser-savvy reader/instructor can disprove the stated symptom for the shown markup. Affected: 05.mdx Opening Case (line 20), Core Concept (line 28), Worked Example Step 1 (lines 44-51), Textbook Walkthrough (line 93); 05.practice.json artifact_signal stem/explanation (lines 11,19); 05.misconceptions.json browser_blamed pattern.
final_opportunities.proposed_change:
Recommend option (a): make the unclosed anchor the LAST/only link before body content so the following paragraphs really are swallowed, OR add a paragraph after the nav and remove the second link's correctness so the open reaches non-anchor content. Concretely: change the Step-1 block to a single unclosed nav link followed by a body element, e.g. '
About

Welcome to my portfolio.

' so the open anchor swallows the

. Then the 'everything below turns blue' prose is literally true. If two links are kept, soften the prose: note the parser auto-closes the first anchor at the second , so the visible bug there is the odd/duplicated link rendering, while the runaway-swallow effect occurs when an unclosed anchor is followed by non-anchor content. Keep the practice item (artifact_signal) accurate by mirroring whichever markup is chosen; the option text 'wraps everything until the next close tag' is actually fine because the second is what supplies that next implicit close.

sources.cite: W3C HTML5 Tree construction, 'in body' insertion mode, start tag 'a' rule (W3C WD)
sources.finding: Spec text: 'If the list of active formatting elements contains an element whose tag name is "a" between the end of the list and the last marker... then this is a parse error; act as if an end tag with the tag name "a" had been seen, then remove that element from the list of active formatting elements and the stack of open elements if the end tag didn't already remove it.' I.e., a second <a> start tag implicitly closes the still-open first anchor, so the runaway effect does not reach content past the second <a>.

sources.cite: WHATWG HTML Living Standard, Parsing section (adoption agency algorithm; 'a' is a formatting element)
sources.finding: The 'a' element is in the formatting category placed in the list of active formatting elements; misnested formatting elements are resolved by the adoption agency algorithm, which is what the implicit on a second triggers. Confirms the parser does not nest two anchors.

Suggested replacement sentence: 'The modified dates all read today because the student saved, duplicated, and re-exported all four during the same late-night session, so they cluster to the same day.'

sources.cite: Microsoft Learn / Win32 file times documentation (NTFS access vs. modified time)
sources.finding: The last-write (modified) time is updated only when the file is written, not when it is opened/read; only the last-access time tracks opens, and on Windows last-access updates are disabled by default (NtfsDisableLastAccessUpdate). Confirms that opening a file does not change the date-modified that file managers display.

final_opportunities.gap: The worked example maps the capability 'Summarize data with a pivot table' but its scale-adaptation note is a VLOOKUP absolute-reference fix (=VLOOKUP(A2,$D$2:$E$4000,2,FALSE)). A pivot table does not use VLOOKUP; it aggregates a source data range. The actual scale/far-transfer concern for a pivot is a stale or non-dynamic source range (the pivot silently excludes new rows added past the original range and must be refreshed, or the source must be an Excel Table / dynamic range). The section conflates two distinct Excel mechanics and teaches the wrong adaptation for the named capability. This is verified against current Microsoft documentation: a pivot built on a fixed range does not pick up appended rows and must have its source range reset or be Refreshed; basing it on an Excel Table makes the range expand automatically.

final_opportunities.proposed_change: Add a 2-3 sentence 'Why the boundary is legal, not just preferential' note after Decision Rule item 3 (Boundary check), naming FERPA and COPPA as statutory backing. FERPA: disclosing personally identifiable information (PII) from education records to a third party generally requires prior written consent (34 CFR 99.30); the school-official/contractor exception (34 CFR 99.31) lets a vendor receive PII ONLY for the contracted purpose and bars re-disclosure without consent, so 'sending names off-site' is a consent-bound act, not a preference. COPPA: under the FTC's amended Rule (published Jan 2025, effective June 23, 2025, full compliance by April 22, 2026), operators collecting from under-13 students must obtain verifiable parental consent before disclosing data to third parties or using it for targeted advertising, and may not retain children's data indefinitely (only as long as reasonably necessary). opportunities.gap: The parameter-explorer and surrounding prose compute 'standardized gain = (post - baseline) / SD' and treat it as the trustworthy measure of whether the tool helped. For a graduate audience this is presented without naming what it is or its limits: it is a standardized mean difference (an effect-size-style index), but with paired/pre-post data the appropriate standardizer and the question of statistical reliability (n, paired SD, sampling error) are non-trivial. The prose says the standardized gain 'shrinks as the spread widens' and frames it as what makes a gain 'dependable,' which risks implying it is a significance test or a settled effect size. With n=22 and no inference, a single standardized gain does not establish dependability.
opportunities.proposed_change: Add one clarifying sentence (and optionally tune the self-explain answer) noting that the standardized gain is an effect-size-style index that helps you read the size of a change relative to spread, but it is not a significance test and a small sample can still produce an unstable estimate; the auditable move is to report n, the baseline, and the spread so a reader can judge reliability, not to treat the ratio as proof. Avoid overclaiming 'dependable improvement' from the ratio alone.
